title: The Night the Library Whispered
blurb: Strange whispers drift through the town library after dark. Ama and her cousin decide to find the ghost.

chapters.title: Whispers After Dark
chapters.text:
The old library in Accra was Ama's favourite place. It smelled of paper and polish, and Mrs Boateng the librarian knew every book by heart. Ama came every afternoon to read.

On Tuesday, Mrs Boateng looked pale. "Something strange is happening," she whispered. "When I lock up at night and come back in the morning, I find books on the floor. And last night, the caretaker heard a voice in the empty reading room."

"What did the voice say?" asked Ama.

"Shh, quiet please," said Mrs Boateng. "That is exactly what it said."

Ama's cousin Kwesi dropped his comic. "A library ghost!" he cried. Ama grinned. "Or a mystery," she said. "Tonight, we are going to find out."

chapters.title: The Stake-Out
chapters.text:
That night, Ama and Kwesi told their parents they were having a sleepover at Mrs Boateng's house next door. Mrs Boateng secretly gave them the library key. "Be careful," she said, "and do not touch anything."

At ten o'clock, the cousins tiptoed into the dark reading room. They hid behind a big sofa with a torch, a notebook and a packet of biscuits.

The library was very still. The clock ticked. A tap dripped. Kwesi's stomach growled loudly. "Shh!" said Ama.

Suddenly something rustled high above them. Both children froze. Then came a soft, scratchy sound, like someone clearing a throat.

chapters.title: Feathers
chapters.text:
Ama slowly raised her torch. The beam travelled up the tall shelves to the very top. There, between two dusty encyclopaedias, sat a pair of round, shining eyes.

"A ghost?" whispered Kwesi, hiding his face behind a cushion.

"No," said Ama, and she began to laugh. "Look at its feathers."

It was a large grey parrot with a bright red tail. It looked down at them and tilted its head. Then it opened its curved beak and said in a perfect, stern voice, "Shh! Quiet please!"

The cousins burst out laughing. They laughed so hard that they had to hold on to each other. "Our ghost," gasped Kwesi, "is a bird!"

chapters.title: The Professor
chapters.text:
Ama made a gentle clucking sound and held out a biscuit. The parrot hopped down the shelf, one step at a time, and took the biscuit from her fingers.

"He must be someone's pet," said Ama. Around his leg was a thin metal ring. On it was a tiny label: Professor, 14 Mango Street.

"Mrs Boateng says that Mr Darko lives on Mango Street," said Kwesi. "He has a pet parrot, and last week it escaped through a window."

"Poor Professor," said Ama. "He must have flown into the library. It is quiet and warm, and he has been listening to Mrs Boateng every day. That is why he sounds just like her."

The parrot sat on Ama's shoulder and began to eat his biscuit.

chapters.title: Case Closed
chapters.text:
The next morning, Ama and Kwesi carried Professor to Mr Darko's house. The old man opened the door and gasped. Then he cried happy tears. "My Professor! I looked for you everywhere!"

The parrot flapped his wings and said, "Hello, hello! Shh, quiet please!" Everyone laughed.

Mr Darko thanked the children and promised to bring Mrs Boateng a basket of mangoes. Then he looked at the ring on the parrot's leg. "I will add my phone number to this label," he said, "in case he ever flies away again."

That afternoon, the library was calm. Mrs Boateng whispered a thank you to Ama and Kwesi. High on the shelf, one small feather was left behind, and Ama kept it as a souvenir.
